Begin with the rationale workbook and tutor feedback. Leave the next slide visible while groups work and circulate to review rationales. Introduce the Gorilla tasks and trial sequences after the break, rather than at the start.

Prioritise rationale review during the first half. NOW’s stated deadline is the end of this session, not the break. A group that still needs work on its rationale can continue it; a group already signed off can begin the method workbook and plan its design.

After the break, give a brief walkthrough of the supplied tasks and one trial sequence, then show the template-adaptation options. No individual responses or common progress reports are required. Students remain at different stages.

Both workbooks and ethics need approval before students modify Gorilla. Watching a preview and discussing an implementation are planning activities, not permission to start editing a task.

What happens on a trial?

Describe the order, timing and response.

Choose the task using the buttons above the diagram. All three task diagrams are available on this one slide, with one displayed at a time. Use Prospect Theory as the shared example to identify the order, timing and response, then continue to the adaptation options. There is no need to walk the whole class through every task.

Prospect Theory: point out the 500 ms blank screen, followed by the scenario, options and preference slider together. The diagram illustrates the trial rather than every interface control. In the current public template participants select a rating and click Next on the response screen; Next is not an additional screen. The instructions define 0 as definitely A and 100 as definitely B.

Time perception: walk through the target and reproduced intervals. Participants press the spacebar once to switch the bulb on and again to end reproduction; this is not a press-and-hold response. Describe the bulb states, target durations, response and recorded reproduction time. Report the timings and any additional intervals in the final task alongside practice, blocks and trial order.

Emotion ratings: the face and slider appear together after the 500 ms blank. Describe what appears, the rating question and scale endpoints, how the participant advances, and the image set, manipulations, practice and trial order used in the final study.

The original supplied diagrams are retained unchanged. Students should describe the final version they actually use, rather than copying a template description without checking it.

Use the topic buttons to choose a template. The table and implementation notes change in place, without leaving this slide. These examples build on the Week 8 materials; the suggestions need a literature-based rationale and tutor approval.

Source: Week 8 Prospect Theory slides 10–11 and NOW Model 2. Slide 10 explicitly offers probability, decision domain, self/other, stakes and time pressure. The two examples shown are self/other decisions and time pressure, which can use the existing scenario layout and slider. The video slide asks for gain/loss framing, while the Week 8 NOW text also allows literature-led changes to the starting factors and outcome. Do not invent an extra rule from these examples; discuss a group’s proposed change against the module guidance. These examples use the template’s gain/loss preference-slider comparison.

Text-based changes can use the existing bindings: scenario_text, option_a and option_b on Trials, Screen 2. For each experimental row, edit the appropriate text and label the second factor in IV2. That label is for data coding: it does not itself change what participants see.

Self/other implementation: create matched scenario versions in which the same decision is made for the participant versus a specified other person. Update pronouns and ownership in the scenario and both options consistently, keeping stakes and probabilities fixed. Specify who the other person is and their relationship to the participant; do not change that relationship at the same time. The slider and response screen can remain.

Time-pressure implementation has two routes. A matched urgency sentence can be added to scenario_text without a new response screen; this manipulates described urgency. An actual deadline requires adding a Time Limit component to the Screen tab for Trials, Screen 2, and binding duration to a new DeadlineMs spreadsheet column. The existing blank Screen 1 is not the screen to limit. A countdown is a separate optional object; keep its format constant if comparing deadline lengths. Pilot the full vignettes: in this template the deadline includes reading and rating. Test both on-time responses and timeouts, then inspect the export before deciding how incomplete responses will be treated. Timeouts may need changes to the supplied analysis code.

Crucial Week 8 instruction, slide 11: avoid showing the same scenario in both frames to the same person. For this class’s within-participant designs, use different scenarios for the two frames and counterbalance which scenario receives which frame across participants. Keeping paired versions merely in separate blocks is not enough to satisfy that advice. Build participant versions of the supplied spreadsheet or use an approved assignment method. Every participant still needs all four factor combinations; the scenario versions they see can differ between participant versions. Extend assignment to the new manipulation so an item set is not permanently tied to one condition.

Technical guidance: Gorilla Binding Guide and Screen Timelimit and Countdown. The public templates inspected use Task Builder 2. These suggested adaptations have not been built or tested in a cloned task.

Source: Week 8 Time Perception slides 4, 6–10 and 12, and Week 8 NOW Model 1. These introduce attention, working memory, emotion and stress. Week 8 permits literature-based changes to the supplied factors and outcome; retaining short/long duration here is an example, not an additional requirement. Work from the supplied reproduction template and discuss changes to its output with a tutor.

Before building, specify the process and the interaction prediction from the group’s reading. A reversal is not required. Both factors have two levels and all participants experience all four combinations. If the group replaces duration as a factor, varied target durations are still needed; implement the two chosen factors explicitly rather than retaining the old short/long labels by accident.

If a group proposes time pressure for the lightbulb task, work out which task demand would actually create it. A reproduction cutoff can force shorter responses, while a numerical countdown can become a timing aid. A general urgency story does not itself establish a useful time-pressure manipulation. The memory-load and emotional-image options connect more directly to the timing task.

Memory implementation: insert an equally timed digit screen before the sequence and a recall screen afterwards, in both experimental displays. Bind the sequence to a new MemoryItems column; label load in IV2. Pilot sequence lengths and display time. In this version memory is maintained through encoding and reproduction, so the manipulation is not encoding-only. Keep recall separate from the spacebar response. New recall data may require changes to filtering in the taught analysis code.

Emotional-image implementation: the current Duration screen shows LightOn.jpg, with time bound to the Duration spreadsheet column. Replace that image setting with a binding to a new TimedImage column in both Block_1 and Block_2. Upload matched, mild emotional/neutral stimuli and enter the filenames and level labels in the spreadsheet. Apply the image manipulation to target presentation only in this example; keep the reproduction screen neutral. Do not replace every bulb image automatically: applying emotion during reproduction as well tests a different question. Adapt instructions and practice to explain the new timed event. All stimuli need the usual tutor approval.

Cross the new levels with each retained duration category and distribute the same target-duration values across them. Block_1 and Block_2 each contain short and long trials: changing only one display would confound the new condition with block. Adapt both, then plan randomisation, counterbalancing and trial counts. Define the chosen accuracy/error score; absolute error, proportional error and variability are different outcomes. A raw difference in reproduced duration is not automatically a difference in accuracy.

Week 8 provides the starting literature, including the attentional-gate account and Gil and Droit-Volet (2011) on emotion effects depending on the temporal task. Use the supplied reading and students’ further sources rather than treating any example here as a ready-made prediction.

Source: Week 8 AdaptiveEmotions slides 5–6 and NOW Model 3. The slides explicitly offer expression, actor sex, social context and body position. NOW allows other emotions and a literature-based change of outcome, but specifically requires retaining a slider because the cleaning code relies on it. The two examples shown are social context and actor sex. They retain happy/neutral expressions for convenience, not as a new prohibition on other expressions.

Context implementation: insert a context screen before the existing 500 ms blank screen in Trials. Add text bound to a new ContextText column plus a continue button. Write matched, mild positive/neutral event descriptions about the pictured person; label context in IV2. Keep presentation format and detail comparable. Both expression categories must appear in both contexts. Students should use their reading to explain why context could change the expression contrast, rather than simply predicting higher ratings for all positive-context trials.

Actor-sex implementation: use a documented stimulus set and its category metadata, rather than guessing categories from appearance. The Week 8 example is typically implemented with male/female actor categories; specify exactly how the selected database defines its labels. Populate stimulus with selected filenames and IV2 with the category label. Include both happy and neutral expressions within each category, with comparable image presentation and multiple actors. Each participant sees both actor categories, so this remains within-participant; it is not a grouping of participants by their own sex or gender. Actor identity varies with actor category, so use a defensible matched selection and acknowledge remaining stimulus differences.

If expressions change, update the selected image files and first-factor labels. If the rated construct changes, update the task instructions and the slider’s left/right labels on Trials, Screen 2 so the question, endpoints and intended outcome agree. Preserve a slider and inspect the export; do not replace it with categorical emotion buttons or assume the cleaning code handles a new format. A new score or scale configuration may require analysis adjustments. Week 8’s outcome is the perceived happiness of the pictured face.

The template’s image is already bound to stimulus. Its current instructions and slider labels are fixed in the display, so spreadsheet changes alone will not update those. Adding a label in IV2 does not change the stimulus or wording. Preview every condition and check a sample export, especially if new screens create additional rows. New emotional stimuli need the usual tutor approval.

Why matching your stimuli matters

An illustrative mismatch: photos selected for “happy” and “neutral” conditions.

Expression changes alongside the setting, lighting and number of people.

A better comparison: use comparable face portraits, with matched backgrounds, lighting and image size. Balance who appears across conditions.

These are actual stock photographs chosen to make a poor comparison visible, not a validated stimulus set or a recommendation to use them in a study. The condition names are proposed labels, not validated emotion classifications. The group photo shows smiling people in a social outdoor scene; the portrait is a single non-smiling person indoors. Differences include setting, light, social contact, number of people, identity, pose, clothing, framing and face size.

If the two conditions use photos like these, an observed difference cannot be attributed specifically to expression. These other features systematically vary with the proposed expression condition. Explain the link between the visual difference and the alternative explanation; variation that does not systematically track a condition may instead add noise.

The repair is to select comparable portraits from a documented image set, matching presentation and background, using a defensible selection rule and balancing identities as appropriate. A named database does not guarantee a matched subset. Even the same person’s smiling and neutral expressions can differ in pose or illumination, so inspect the actual files.

Photos: RDNE Stock project, Pexels photo 7551181; Cindy Bartillon, Pexels photo 35633642. Source links are under each photo. Downloaded under the Pexels licence on 23 November 2026. Photographs are embedded in the HTML for offline presentation and are displayed without image-content edits.

Use this example during a relevant group conversation; no response from the room is required. Transfer the question to other topics: does wording length vary with frame, or does visibility change alongside a timing manipulation? What else changes with the condition?

Why use each person as their own comparison?

Illustrative happiness ratings (0–100): some people tend to rate higher than others.

Different people

Person Happy Neutral
Alex 80 —
Sam — 40

The 40-point gap can include differences in usual mood or rating habits.

The same people

Person Happy Neutral
Alex 80 70
Sam 50 40

Happy − neutral = 10 for each person.

Everyone completes all four conditions. Plan trial order and any repeated items.

All groups in this lab are using within-participant designs. Use this illustration if a group needs to explain the benefit of comparing each participant with themselves. It does not introduce a choice between within, between and mixed designs.

The invented ratings make the issue concrete. If Alex sees only happy faces and Sam sees only neutral faces, the observed gap is 40 points. In the fuller illustration, Alex also rates neutral faces 70 and Sam rates happy faces 50: the happy-minus-neutral difference is 10 for each person. Stable differences in typical ratings can obscure the comparison when different people provide the two condition scores.

A properly randomised between-participant design is valid; it is not inherently confounded simply because different participants take part. Randomisation balances participant characteristics in expectation, but individual differences can make the comparison less precise, especially in small samples. These two fictional people illustrate that issue, not a statistical test or a recommendation about sample size.

The same-person comparison removes stable additive differences in typical ratings from each person’s contrast. It does not remove stimulus confounds, all differences in scale use, order effects or carry-over. The lighting and setting problem on the preceding slide still needs its own control.

The example focuses on happy versus neutral faces. In the students’ full 2 × 2 within-participant designs, each participant experiences all four combinations. The practical questions are how to organise trials and blocks, handle repeated items, and reduce practice, awareness or emotional carry-over.

For prospect theory, Week 8 slide 11 advises showing different scenarios in each frame and counterbalancing scenario-to-frame assignment across participants. The Week 10 material describes separating paired versions by blocks; block separation alone does not prevent recognition. Use the Week 8 assignment advice when adapting the template. Randomisation cannot repair stimuli that systematically differ in other ways.

Selecting stimuli and checking controls

Method workbook: sections 4e, 5d and 7–8

Start with the template’s stimuli. Try a few candidate items or item sets and show how you would use them across conditions.

Potential problem Why it matters Planned control
Happy photos are brighter. Brightness varies with expression and could affect ratings. Use comparable images; record how brightness and presentation are matched.

For your materials, record the source and selection rule, one plausible competing explanation, and your control.

Explain one limitation that remains. Ask a tutor to check the suitability of your stimuli.

Use this slide when a group is selecting materials or evaluating a possible confound. A few examples can help scrutinise a selection rule; there is no required quota to produce in this session. An item set contains the versions needed for a comparison, depending on the manipulation. The total number of stimuli and trials requires its own justification.

Ask how the selected examples represent the intended construct and why these particular items were chosen. Previous studies, methods sections and documented stimulus sets can support a selection rule. For a stimulus database, record relevant ratings or norms and how the subset was chosen.

The live Open Materials listing identifies the FEI Face Database as the source for the emotion template. This is a research collection of face photographs from Centro Universitário FEI in Brazil, including neutral and smiling frontal views. This provides a concrete selection exercise: inspect the supplied faces and explain the intended subset and controls. A named database alone does not establish validity for the chosen emotional outcome or guarantee that conditions are matched. Use Week 8’s topic examples when planning an extension; the starting factors and outcomes are not all compulsory. The emotion task must retain a slider as stated in Week 8.

Check the distinction between keeping a feature constant, matching its distribution across conditions and counterbalancing item versions. A remaining limitation should be written down rather than hidden by a claim that all confounds have been eliminated.

For timing tasks, identify the timed event and use varied durations rather than endlessly repeating one duration. For framing tasks, preserve equivalent outcomes when comparing the gain/loss versions. For emotion tasks, use mild stimuli and obtain tutor approval.

Groups can divide work once they agree the design: one person searches for candidate materials, one records the controls, and another checks the relevant methods literature. Bring the decisions together before editing the workbook.

Writing your method

Method workbook: sections 2, 6c and 9–11

Participants

Record recruitment, criteria and a target sample. Use the NOW sample-size guidance and discuss feasibility with a tutor.

Procedure

Specify practice, blocks, trials per condition, ordering and total duration. Record participant numbers and trial numbers separately.

Ethics and evaluation

Adapt the Experimental information, consent and debrief templates. Record your design choices, justifications and remaining limitations.

Add these decisions to the workbook. Keep track of what still needs tutor approval.

The workbook requires a realistic recruitment route; the participant pool is not available for this project. Discuss target population, reach, inclusion/exclusion criteria and relevant device or language requirements. Do not confuse participants with trials or assume more trials replaces a sample-size justification.

NOW gives a deliberately crude planning exercise using pwr.f2.test with u = 1, f2 = .15, power = .80 and sig.level = .05, and explicitly describes its limits. Keep that detail in NOW and the tutor conversation. Explain the effect-size assumption and discuss the actual within-participant design and recruitment target with a tutor. The prescribed calculation is a rough planning exercise rather than a guarantee of power for the actual task.

For procedure, ask what happens from the study link through information, consent, instructions, practice, experimental trials and debrief. How were block order, item versions and condition order decided? Why those trial numbers? Are instructions and online-device requirements appropriate?

Use the Experimental versions of participant-facing templates. In accordance with the supplied module guidance, use mild emotional stimuli only and obtain tutor approval. Adapt the relevant emotional-stimuli information to the actual study, and discuss additional demographic questions with a tutor. Read the module-level ethics agreement before signing the ethics form.

Use this slide when a group is ready to document recruitment, procedure or ethics. The completed method workbook requires at least three design choices, their justifications and limitations in section 11; that is a workbook requirement, not a target for this work period. Groups can draw on their existing decisions and use the replication checklist to identify what remains unclear.

Checks for your chosen topic

Topic Check before changing it
Time perception Make the timed event clear. Use varied durations and explain what is reproduced and scored.
Prospect theory For gain/loss framing, preserve equivalent outcomes. Use different scenarios per frame for each person; counterbalance scenario-to-frame assignment.
Emotion Check the face photos supplied in the template. Retain a slider. If changing the expression or rating question, update the stimuli, instructions and endpoint labels. Use tutor-approved stimuli.

Templates and previews: Gorilla Open Materials.
Full requirements: NOW → Week 10 → The experimental tasks and the task checklist in Important files.

Use these checks for each group’s topic. It condenses task-specific constraints from the supplied NOW content; it is not a substitute for the full task checklist.

Time perception: the example duration manipulation uses short and long ranges. If replacing that manipulation, NOW advises a single duration range across the task while still including different durations. Inspect the supplied response procedure and output before defining the score.

Prospect theory: the actual template contrasts equivalent monetary outcomes described as gains or losses. This differs from Week 9’s invented holiday discount/extra-charge demonstration, which was not a pure framing manipulation. Week 8 slide 11 advises different scenarios in each frame for each person, counterbalancing scenario-to-frame assignment across participants. Implement that assignment in the template rather than relying on block separation alone.

Emotion: report the rating question and configured response scale used in the final study.

Before you leave: workbook check

Rationale workbook · sections 1–6: complete all sections, including the final self-check, and get tutor sign-off today.

After rationale sign-off, work on the Method workbook at your group’s stage:

Method sections What to record
1, 3–5 Your task, outcome measure and both manipulations: levels, implementation and justification.
6–8 Design and trial order, selected stimuli and materials, and controls for confounds.

Record which method sections are complete, what still needs deciding and your next actions. The whole method workbook need not be finished today.

NOW: Design · Tasks and stimuli · Sample size · Gorilla guides · Workbooks and ethics

Required end-of-session completion: the first, Literature Review and Rationale Workbook, sections 1–6, must be complete and signed off by at least one tutor. The section numbers come from the supplied workbook: model/design, first literature search, interaction rationale, aims and hypotheses, integrated rationale, and final self-check.

The Method Workbook has no shared section-completion deadline in the supplied Week 10 guidance. The original slides ask students to progress it and potentially finalise it. The section groups here are a practical map for today’s work after rationale sign-off, not an extra requirement to finish a fixed set before leaving.

Method section 1 covers the task; section 3 the outcome and scoring; sections 4–5 the two manipulations; section 6 the design, blocks and trials; section 7 materials and stimulus selection; section 8 controls. These map closely to the session’s focus on operationalising the design and choosing stimuli. Groups can work on a difficult decision in any of these sections rather than rushing through the list.

Method section 2 covers the sample and justification; section 9 the procedure and instructions; section 10 ethics and tutor approval of stimuli; section 11 design evaluation and the replication check. Progress these as the relevant decisions become clear. Ethics work can proceed alongside design work; it does not need to wait until every earlier section is finished.

Before leaving, each group should record its completed sections, unresolved decisions, who will do the remaining work and any feedback or approvals still needed. Both workbooks and ethics must be approved before modifying Gorilla, and the experiment also needs approval before data collection.

The NOW links retain the design, task, sample-size, Gorilla and document guidance. For additional demographic questions, use Demographic information and discuss the need with a tutor.
